lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In nineteen seventy nine a tribunal in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, charged that about three million people had been killed, under a regime that lasted three years, eight months and twenty days.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand fourteen a second court in the same city put every estimate between six hundred thousand and three million, and the accepted ones between one and a half and two million.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Three million charged, two million at most accepted, and a list the prison kept itself.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Cambodian genocide, nineteen seventy five to nineteen seventy nine.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The seventeenth of April, nineteen seventy five. Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, in Southeast Asia, between Vietnam and Thailand.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Khmer Rouge, a communist movement led by Saloth Sar, known as Pol Pot, have taken the city from its military government. Their state will call itself Democratic Kampuchea.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Within forty eight hours the soldiers march at least two million people out at gunpoint, saying it is for three days, until the Americans stop bombing.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The United States bombed eastern Cambodia from nineteen sixty nine to nineteen seventy three; it had already stopped.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Chum Mey, a mechanic, walks out asking to see Angkar and is told to move on; he could not find, he said, who Angkar was.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Chum Mey, in two thousand nine, to the court that tried the regime, as the transcript renders him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: And as a result, my son died. Where upon then I borrowed a hoe and then I dug the ground and buried my son. He was two years old at the time.

segments.author: Chum Mey
segments.work: testimony as a civil party, Case 001 transcript, in the court's English

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Phnom Penh, the emptied city, in the years that follow. A former high school has become Security Prison Twenty One, S-21, called Tuol Sleng.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Vann Nath, a painter, arrives blindfolded and cuffed to another prisoner, and the blindfold comes off in front of a camera.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Vann Nath, to the court, as the transcript renders him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: And after we arrived into a room we were each photographed. After they took off the blindfold I saw the camera in front of my face already.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The prison hands out shorts with nothing to tighten the waist, so that nobody can hang himself.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Then the prison asks what he is good at. Vann Nath is kept alive to paint portraits of Pol Pot; he told the court why he chose to.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Of course, the colour portrait could save my life. If I made the portrait attractive, then the Angkar would be pleased with the painting; then I would be spared from being executed.

segments.author: Vann Nath
segments.work: testimony as a witness, Case 001 transcript, in the court's English

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Phnom Penh, thirty years on. A court Cambodia set up with the United Nations to try the regime reads the prison's own lists of who came in and who was executed, a hundred and seven duplicates struck out.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Trial Chamber, the judges who heard the case, in July of two thousand ten.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The Revised S-21 Prisoner List indicates that no fewer than 12,273 individuals were detained at S-21.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five thousand nine hundred and ninety four entries are men, one thousand six hundred and ninety eight women, eighty nine children. Four thousand four hundred and ninety two carry neither a sex nor an age.

segments.author: Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, Trial Chamber

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The commandant of the prison, Kaing Guek Eav, called Duch, spoke to the court of a photograph of himself training cadres, the party's own people.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: It is shocking and upsetting to see that picture of me, I who killed more than 12,300 people. I am accountable for all the crimes committed at S-21.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Three million charged, two million at most accepted, and a list the prison kept itself.

segments.author: Kaing Guek Eav, called Duch
segments.work: statement before the Trial Chamber, as the court compiled it in English

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: January nineteen seventy nine. A Vietnamese army is taking Phnom Penh; the regime is fleeing west. At the prison it is the last morning.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Vann Nath walks out of the painting workshop in a single line with woodcrafters, electricians and blacksmiths, about thirteen men, not tied, not handcuffed. No other prisoners remain.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The event record puts the survivors at between seven and twelve; the court wrote only that a very small number survived.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: His wife and two children had been left at a cooperative, one of the regime's farms, the eldest five, the youngest six months. Vann Nath, as the transcript renders him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: After I was freed and after I returned I learned that my children died.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Only his wife survived.

segments.author: Vann Nath
segments.work: testimony as a witness, Case 001 transcript, in the court's English

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Phnom Penh, August nineteen seventy nine. The government Vietnam has installed holds a tribunal and charges about three million dead, on a survey of one city, one commune, and a journalist's figures from three provinces.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Nobody knows how many died. What exists is a set of counts that disagree, each with a name on it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In nineteen ninety nine three experts the United Nations General Assembly had asked for put the scholars at one and a half million and nearly one point seven million, about twenty per cent of the population. Historians, they wrote, had rejected two to three million.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand fourteen the Trial Chamber surveyed the estimates it had been given, and wrote this.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Overall, estimates indicate that between 600,000 and 3 million died as a result of Khmer Rouge policies and actions. Within this range, experts accept estimates falling between 1.5 and 2 million excess deaths as the most accurate.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand eighteen the same court added that the absence of reliable statistical data leaves inherent uncertainty around any number. This programme states no single number.

segments.author: Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, Trial Chamber

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Phnom Penh, the same August. The tribunal defines genocide by decree, to include forced evacuation, forced labour and the abolition of religion, and finds it committed against the whole people.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In nineteen ninety nine the experts apply the genocide convention of nineteen forty eight instead, the treaty that defines the crime as acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: They name the Cham, Cambodia's Muslim minority, the Vietnamese and the Buddhist monkhood, and stop at the Khmer, the majority.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The experts, on the Khmer national group.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The Group does not take a position on this issue, but believes that any tribunal will have to address this question should Khmer Rouge officials be charged with genocide against the Khmer national group.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand eighteen the court answered for two groups: the Cham, targeted throughout; the Vietnamese, for expulsion until late nineteen seventy six and for destruction from April nineteen seventy seven.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The killing of the Khmer majority was charged as crimes against humanity, not as genocide.

segments.author: Group of Experts for Cambodia
segments.work: report transmitted by the Secretary-General, paragraph 65

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: One of the court's own judges, You Ottara, wrote separately: the case had focused exclusively on the killing of Vietnamese and Cham, and the reasons had never been explained.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: In my view, the resulting approach which the Trial Chamber has necessarily followed is much too narrow.

segments.author: Judge You Ottara
segments.work: separate opinion appended to the Case 002/02 Judgement, paragraph 4469

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five accounts of who did this, who stopped it, and what to call it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: They are argued from what this programme could read: the court's judgments and transcripts, the tribunal's papers of nineteen seventy nine, one day of the United Nations Security Council, the experts' report, one interview, a demographer's figures.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The books could not be read here. Each gets its own case first.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The first account is the regime's own; the record holds it in one statement to the Security Council and one interview.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It begins with the American bombing.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Days after Phnom Penh fell, the delegate of Democratic Kampuchea told the Council his country was the victim of flagrant aggression by Vietnam.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In nineteen ninety seven Pol Pot, asked by the journalist Nate Thayer whether he would apologise, answered no. On the dead, to Thayer.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: To say that millions died is too much. Another aspect you have to know is that Vietnamese agents, they were there. There was rice, but they didn't give rice to the population

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The second account is the survivors', and the record holds two of them, both men.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Chum Mey was beaten for twelve days and nights, the court found, electrocuted twice, and had two toenails pulled out. He described his cell, as the two thousand eighteen judgment quotes him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The situation was so miserable. I thought that I was being treated worse than a human being, I was treated like an animal, like a dog. A dog would be given steamed rice to eat, but for me, I was given only watery gruel.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: No woman who lived through the regime speaks in this record in her own words.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The third account is Vietnam's, given to the Security Council on the same day as the regime's.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The experts date a border war between the two from nineteen seventy five, and raids that massacred hundreds of Vietnamese villagers from nineteen seventy seven. The invasion began on the twenty fifth of December, nineteen seventy eight.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Ha Van Lau, for Vietnam, told the Council there were two wars to distinguish, and named the regime as Vietnam named it, the Pol Pot-Ieng Sary clique.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: one, the border war started by the Pol Pot-Ieng Sary clique against Viet Nam, which the Vietnamese people have been forced to deal with, the other, the revolutionary war of the Kampuchean people against the dictatorial rule of the Pol Pot-Ieng Sary clique

segments.title: Viet Nam and the Vietnamese Liberation

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fourth account belongs to the court and the scholars; it is an account of limits.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The court convicted three people: Duch in two thousand ten, and in two thousand eighteen Nuon Chea, called Brother Number Two, and Khieu Samphan, the head of state.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the dead, the scholarship turned the count into a distribution. Patrick Heuveline, a demographer, in two thousand fifteen.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The median value of 1.9 million excess deaths represents 21 percent of the population at risk.

segments.title: The ECCC Tribunal and the Demographers

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fifth account is about what the world did next, and the record holds one day of it, the eleventh of January, nineteen seventy nine, at the Security Council.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That day the Chinese delegate called the invasion a large-scale naked armed aggression, with Soviet support; the Soviet delegate called the regime's rule a policy of open genocide.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The delegate of the United States, on whether the regime should be heard at all.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: We make no judgements one way or the other. We just think that that Government has a right to be heard.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The regime kept the seat of Cambodia at the United Nations until nineteen ninety one. The account holds that the United States encouraged China to support it; the words are secondhand.

segments.title: The Regional Intervention and the Cold War

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Each is true as far as it goes.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The regime's account never mentions the ethnic Vietnamese inside Cambodia, the registers its own prison kept, or the commandant who said he killed more than twelve thousand three hundred.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The account of the survivors is two men who saw the regime from inside its prison; no Cham, no Vietnamese and no base person, a peasant of the party's old zones, speaks in this record.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Vietnamese account has two wars in it and no room for the third, the one its own army fought.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The account of the court reaches two minorities, and its own judge wrote that nobody explained why.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Cold War account holds the statements of one day and no resolution.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And the one count read entry by entry was kept by the men who ran the prison.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Khmer Rouge held Cambodia from the seventeenth of April, nineteen seventy five, until a Vietnamese army took Phnom Penh in January nineteen seventy nine. A court convicted three men.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The law that made the court ends the period on the sixth of January, nineteen seventy nine. The last judgment, in two thousand twenty two, ends it on the seventh.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Between those dates, that judgment says, over a million people died, and without the documentary evidence that remained there would be nothing but the testimony of elderly, traumatised survivors and the bones of the dead.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Three million charged, two million at most accepted, and a list the prison kept itself.
